proxy_language: Classical Armenian (Grabar), with Old Georgian as secondary comparandum and Commagenian Greek/Iranian theonyms (Nemrud Dag inscription) for court and cult vocabulary
proxy_rationale: The label combines Armenia, Georgia and Commagene: a Hellenistic-Iranian court culture of fire-cult, mountain sanctuaries and royal tombs (Antiochus I of Commagene, Armenian Artaxiads/Arsacids, Iberian Kartli). Armenian is the best-attested language of the core region, rich in Iranian loanwords (Parthian) for court, religion and rank. Old Georgian (5th c. onward) is attested later but a defensible Kartvelian proxy for Iberia/Colchis. Commagene texts are in Greek, so Armenian (with Iranian-derived court and cult terms) is the main proxy and Georgian a flavour option. Link to any single 'court' is indirect, hence medium.
phonology: Classical Armenian consonants: stops/affricates in three series (voiceless aspirated p' t' c' ch' k', voiced b d dz j g, voiceless unaspirated/ejective-reflex p t c ch k), fricatives s z sh zh x gh h v, sonorants m n r (trill) rr l, y. Vowels: a e i o u and the schwa-like ə (often unwritten). Old Georgian: five vowels a e i o u; ejectives p' t' k' q' c' ch' alongside aspirated p t k and voiced b d g; uvular q, gh, x; clusters allowed (e.g. mts-, bgh-, tskh-).
phonotactics: Armenian: syllables (C)(C)V(C)(C); initial clusters occur (sk-, st-, sp-, kr-, tr-, pr-), but many Iranian loans keep clusters like 'ast-'; in native words an epenthetic ə-/e- is inserted before initial r- (erkir 'earth', erku 'two'). Words end in vowels or consonants (-n, -r, -s, -k', -ts). Stress falls on the last syllable (or penult before a final ə). Georgian: heavy consonant clusters (gvprtskvni), no stress effect on spelling. Native Armenian words rarely start with vowel+r clusters.
orthography: Use the standard scholarly Hubschmann/Meillet Latin transliteration of Classical Armenian: aspirates written with an apostrophe or modifier (p' t' k' c' ch'), plus sh zh gh kh dz. For a simplified audit Latin spelling, use plain digraphs: ch, sh, zh, gh, kh, dz and treat aspirates as unmarked. Georgian: Latin romanization (national system) with apostrophe for ejectives optional.
morphology: Armenian nouns decline for seven cases (nom, acc, gen, dat, abl, instr, loc) and two numbers (plural -k' / -er, -ner later); stems vowel-final (a-, i-, o-, u-stems) or consonantal. Genitive often -i, -oy, -u; ablative -e/-ê; instrumental -ov. Derivational suffixes: -ut'iwn (abstract, 'ness'), -ik (diminutive), -ean (patronymic/belonging), -akan (adjectival), -ar (agent/place), -ean, -ik. Adjectives follow agreement-free rules (no gender; case endings only). Georgian: agglutinative prefix-suffix morphology; nominal suffixes -i (nom), -is (gen), -s (dat), -it (instr); circumfix mi-...-eli for agents.
compounding: Armenian compounds are head-final with a linking vowel -a- or -o- (-a- after most stems): erkir-a-gund 'globe', mard-a-sirt 'man-loving'. Examples: hur 'fire' + hrdeh; sar 'mountain/ridge' + berd 'fortress'. The genitive construction 'X of Y' is Y-genitive + X (e.g. tun azgi 'house of the nation'), but name-compounds typically use the linking vowel: Y-a-X (Ara-mazd, Vahagn, Mihr-a-kan 'of Mithra'). Agent nouns: stem + -ich or -ol ('maker' type). Georgian compounds also head-final with -a-/-o- linkers (mta-mtsvane).
noun_phrase_order: Armenian: adjective before noun (Classical: bari 'good' + nom; mets 'great' + t'agavor 'king'), genitive before head (Hayots' ashkharh 'the land of the Armenians'); demonstratives precede. Georgian: adjective and genitive also precede the head noun. Prepositions are postposed in some Armenian constructions (i + abl).

notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word. The sample strings in the game (Hexyu siva, Moga monak, Genib, Wipbo, Gobyab, Hezi) are not Armenian-like and use unlicensed x/w/y patterns; names should instead use Armenian-style stems with -a-/-o- linkers and genitive -i/-oy/-ean. The Commagene component is only indirectly attested (Greek inscriptions with Iranian theonyms: Oromasdes, Artagnes, Verethragna); for such names use Armenian reflexes (Aramazd, Vahagn, Mihr) rather than invention.
